newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola unity cabinet takes office to end civil war.
newsitem.headline: Angola unity cabinet takes office to end civil war.

text.p: Angola on Friday swore in a government of national unity intended to cement peace between rivals who brought the country to its knees over nearly two decades of civil war.

President Jose Eduardo dos Santos said in a speech at a ceremony attended by 13 foreign heads of state that the new government would be no miracle cure for the country's many ills but added: "It could make a definite contribution towards a better solution."
Jonas Savimbi, leader of the former rebel movement UNITA, failed to attend the inauguration after citing fears for his safety in the capital.
But his deputy, Antonio Dembo, read a speech on Savimbi's behalf in which he called on the new government to carry out its business with openness and a spirit of unity.
"The history of our country is filled with sadness and it has been a long and difficult road to this point," Dembo said.
Among the foreign heads of state watching were President Jorge Sampaio of Portugal -- the former colonial power -- and presidents Nelson Mandela of South Africa and Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe.

"The formation of this government is another fundamental step in a long and difficult process of peace," dos Santos said. "Behind us lie thousands of dead, a devastated country and a semi-paralysed economy."
UNITA has been given portfolios in the unity cabinet -- geology and mining, health, commerce and tourism.
Savimbi himself has been appoined "president of the largest opposition party", a post that carries the right to regular consultation with dos Santos and an official residence in Luanda.
The ceremony on Friday was the culmination of a peace process which began in November 1994 when the two sides signed a pact in Lusaka, Zambia.
The MPLA of dos Santos went to war with UNITA shortly after independence in 1975, turning the oil- and diamond-rich country into one of Africa's basket cases.
Millions of land mines still have to be cleared and a vast task of rebuilding devastated infrastructure awaits the new government.

A stable, lasting peace should allow greater exploitation of the country's largely unexplored mineral wealth and could bring greater regulation to diamond mining, now largely the realm of freelancers under UNITA control.
But diplomats in Luanda cautioned against excessive optimism. They noted a major problem would be extending central government administration to remote parts of the country dominated by UNITA.
"The negotiations on extension of state administration are moving very slowly," said one official close to the peace process. "The issue could very well be a major problem."
U.N. officials this week unveiled a plan to begin demobilising some 40,000 UNITA fighters on Saturday. The soldiers have spent months in U.N. assembly areas.
